notes.title: Start here: a payments lab built around one idempotent endpoint
notes.body:
This repo is a small Next.js + Prisma payments console. Its name comes from `POST /api/payments`, which must create exactly one payment even when a client retries. Around it sit a refund route, a provider webhook, a webhook relay and a reconciliation job.

Read in this order. `docs/learning/concepts-demonstrated.md` names each concept and then says what you actually find in the code, gaps included. `docs/learning/flow-traces.md` follows requests file by file; the numbered flows at the end trace the hardest cases. `docs/architecture/request-lifecycle.md` repeats the traces line by line and lists findings L1-L5. `docs/architecture/auth-and-permissions.md` covers sessions, the role matrix and findings A1-A4. `docs/learning/testing-rationale.md` says which claims were checked and how.

The docs were corrected after review, so trust the line-numbered sections over the short quick maps at the top. For every route you trace, write down which guard (if any) runs first.

excerpts.quote: This section says what you will find when you get there — the specific mechanism, its exact boundary, and the gap a reviewer should notice.

readMore.why: The create path: 192 lines that every idempotency question in this quest is about.
Line-by-line traces A-D and the L-findings.

notes.title: Concept: an idempotency record is a key, a fingerprint and a saved answer
notes.body:
An idempotency key lets a client say "this is the same request as before". The server must then decide three things: is it really the same request, has the first one finished, and what should a repeat return?

In this repo the answer lives in an `IdempotencyRecord` row. It stores the route, the client key, a SHA-256 fingerprint of the request, a status, and the response that was sent. The fingerprint is built by `stableStringify()` in `src/lib/idempotency/requestFingerprint.ts`.

While reading, work out four things for yourself from the code: which columns the unique constraint on the record covers; exactly which value is hashed (the raw request, or something produced after validation); what each branch of `createPaymentWithIdempotency` returns for a repeat whose fingerprint matches, differs, or belongs to an unfinished record; and what actually protects two requests that arrive at the same moment. Also check where the admin console generates its key.

excerpts.quote: ### Idempotency — the concept the repo is named after
model IdempotencyRecord {

readMore.why: The IdempotencyRecord model with its status, lockedAt and response columns.

notes.title: Concept: where the reads sit relative to the transaction
notes.body:
A database transaction only protects what happens inside it. A value you read before `prisma.$transaction(...)` opens can be changed by another request before your writes commit, and nothing will warn you. Interactive Prisma transactions also have a rule about failure: writes made through the `tx` client belong to the transaction, so what survives depends on whether the callback finishes or throws.

This repo has four transactions: payment create, webhook processing, refund and the reconciliation write-out. For each one, make a short table yourself: every read and every write, and whether it happens before the transaction opens, inside it through `tx`, or after it.

Then ask two questions of each path. If two requests run it at the same moment, could both act on the same earlier read? And if something throws halfway through the callback, which of the rows it wrote would still exist afterwards? Answer them from the code in `refundService.ts` and `webhookService.ts`, not from the summaries.

excerpts.quote: ### Transactions as a consistency boundary
return prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {

readMore.why: Trace C walks the refund path step by step.

notes.title: A rolled-back attempt leaves no key behind
notes.body:
**Key: the same 404, after running the whole create again from scratch.**

`createIdempotencyRecord` is called with `tx`, as the first write inside `prisma.$transaction`. The owner check throws `RouteError(404, "OWNER_NOT_FOUND", ...)` inside the same callback, so the whole transaction rolls back, record included. The catch block only handles P2002 and rethrows anything else. On the retry, `findIdempotencyRecord` finds nothing, the transaction runs again, and the owner is still missing.

Why the others are wrong:
- *IN_PROGRESS*: no record survives to be in progress.
- *a stored 404 replay*: only a completed 202 response is ever stored.
- *KEY_REUSED_WITH_DIFFERENT_PAYLOAD*: nothing is stored to compare against, and the body is identical anyway.

excerpts.quote: if (!owner) { throw new RouteError(404, "OWNER_NOT_FOUND", "The selected payment owner does not exist.");

readMore.why: The record is written through tx, inside the transaction.

notes.title: A reused key with a new body is refused up front
notes.body:
The record is found by route and key. Its `requestHash` was computed from the first body; the new body has `amountMinor: 501`, so its fingerprint differs. Line 71 compares them and throws `RouteError(409, "IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED_WITH_DIFFERENT_PAYLOAD", ...)`. This happens before line 86, so no transaction is opened and nothing is written.

- "A replay of the first payment" would only happen if the hashes matched; the service compares the hash, not just the key.
- "A second payment for 501" is exactly what the check prevents: a key may only ever mean one request.
- "400 MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY" is for a request with no header at all (line 62).

excerpts.quote: if (existingRecord.requestHash !== requestHash) {

notes.title: The fingerprint is taken after zod normalizes the body
notes.body:
The route parses the body with `createPaymentSchema` before the service sees it. The currency field is `z.string().trim().length(3).transform((value) => value.toUpperCase())`: " usd" is trimmed to "usd" (length 3, so it passes) and upper-cased to "USD". The service then fingerprints that parsed object, so both requests produce the same hash and the retry is replayed.

- "409 because the raw bytes differ" is wrong: raw bytes are never hashed.
- "400, four characters" is wrong: `.trim()` runs before the `.length(3)` check.
- "Currency is left out of the fingerprint" is wrong: the whole parsed body is hashed.

excerpts.quote: currency: z.string().trim().length(3).transform((value) => value.toUpperCase()),
so `" usd"` and `"USD"` with the same key are treated as the same request, not a mismatch

notes.title: The browser hook mints a key per call
notes.body:
`useCreatePayment()` builds its request inside `mutationFn`, and the header is `"Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID()`. A new UUID is generated every time the mutation runs, so a retry after a timeout is a new key, the server finds no record, and a second payment is created. The idempotency layer only helps API clients that deliberately resend the same key.

- "The same key as before" would need the key stored once per user intent, for example in component state; the docs list that as the fix.
- "No key at all, 400" is wrong: every call sends a header.
- "409 IN_PROGRESS" needs the same key, which the retry does not have.

excerpts.quote: "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID(),
so every submit — including a user's retry after a timeout — is a brand-new key

notes.title: Finding L2: the refund limit is checked on stale numbers
notes.body:
`createRefundForPayment` reads the payment (line 25), sums earlier successful refunds (line 31) and runs `assertRefundAllowed` (line 34), all before `prisma.$transaction` opens at line 36. With two simultaneous requests both read a refunded total of 0, both see 100 remaining, both pass the check, and both insert and succeed: 120 refunded on a 100 charge. Neither flips the payment, because 0 + 60 is not 100.

- "Fails REFUND_AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_CAPTURE inside the transaction" is wrong: the check never runs inside the transaction.
- "Waits on a row lock" is wrong: nothing locks the payment row, and the schema does not bound the sum.
- "Each flips the payment to REFUNDED" is wrong for the same 0 + 60 reason.

excerpts.quote: const refundedAmount = await sumSuccessfulRefundsForPayment(payment.id);
**both succeed, 120 refunded**

notes.title: Fully refunded money, yet the payment still says SUCCEEDED
notes.body:
Inside each transaction the service computes `fullyRefunded = refundedAmount + refund.amountMinor === payment.amountMinor`. `refundedAmount` is the value read before the transaction, which was 0 for both racers. 0 + 50 is not 100, so neither request runs the `REFUNDED` transition. The payment ends `SUCCEEDED` with its full amount refunded, and the UI still offers it as refundable.

- "REFUNDED" would need one request to see the other's refund in its total; neither does.
- "FAILED" is not even a legal move from SUCCEEDED, and no code path tries it here.
- "PENDING until reconciliation" is wrong: reconciliation never corrects state, and nothing moves a payment back to PENDING.

excerpts.quote: const fullyRefunded = refundedAmount + refund.amountMinor === payment.amountMinor;
**100 refunded, payment still `SUCCEEDED`**

notes.title: Staff may create on behalf of a customer
notes.body:
**Key: the customer owns it, and createdByUserId is the OPS user.**

`resolvePaymentOwnerForCreate` returns the requested owner when it differs from the caller only if the caller's role holds `PAYMENT_READ_ANY`. OPS has it, so the customer's id comes back. The service checks that the user exists and then calls `createPayment` with `ownerUserId: owner.id` and `createdByUserId: input.session.userId`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *403 FORBIDDEN_OWNER_OVERRIDE*: that is for a role without `PAYMENT_READ_ANY`, such as CUSTOMER.
- *owned by OPS*: the requested owner is used, not ignored.
- *created by the customer*: the creator is always the session user.

excerpts.quote: if (!roleHasPermission(session.role, Permission.PAYMENT_READ_ANY)) {

readMore.why: Which roles hold PAYMENT_CREATE and PAYMENT_READ_ANY.

notes.title: Finding L3: a rejection written through tx is rolled back
notes.body:
FAILED is terminal, so `assertAllowedPaymentTransition("FAILED", "SUCCEEDED")` throws a 409 inside the transaction. The catch at lines 123-127 calls `markWebhookEventRejected(webhookEvent.id, message, tx)` and then rethrows. Because the error leaves the `prisma.$transaction` callback, Prisma rolls back EVERYTHING written through `tx`: the REJECTED update, the new WebhookEvent row, the provider-mirror update and the WEBHOOK_RECEIVED event.

- "A REJECTED row with the message" is what the code intends, not what survives.
- "The mirror moves to SUCCEEDED" is wrong: that update was also made through `tx`.
- "A WEBHOOK_RECEIVED event" is wrong for the same reason.

Fix shape: record the rejection in a separate write after the failed transaction.

excerpts.quote: await markWebhookEventRejected(webhookEvent.id, message, tx);
Writing an error record through `tx` and then re-throwing (`webhookService.ts:123-127`) erases the error record.

notes.title: Finding L5: an open state-mutation endpoint
notes.body:
The webhook route's `POST` is a plain function: no `withRouteAuth`, no signature check and no schema; the parsed body is passed on through a bare type cast. The service finds the provider mirror and the payment by id, maps REFUNDED to local REFUNDED, and the state machine allows `SUCCEEDED -> REFUNDED`. So the payment and the mirror become REFUNDED and the event trail says `provider-webhook`, but no `Refund` row exists because the refund service was never called.

- "401 UNAUTHENTICATED" is wrong: the route is not wrapped in `withRouteAuth`.
- "409 INVALID_PAYMENT_TRANSITION" is wrong: SUCCEEDED may become REFUNDED.
- "400 VALIDATION_ERROR" is wrong: the webhook has no zod schema at all.

excerpts.quote: const payload = await parseJson(request, (body) => body as Record<string, unknown>);
SUCCEEDED: ["REFUNDED"],

notes.title: Each delivery succeeds or fails on its own
notes.body:
**Key: delivered 1, failed 1, and the third stays PENDING for a later run.**

`deliverPendingWebhooks(limit)` asks `listPendingWebhookDeliveries(limit)` for at most `limit` PENDING rows, oldest first, so only two are selected. The loop wraps each delivery in its own `try/catch`: the first is marked DELIVERED, the second's error is caught and the row is marked FAILED, and the loop goes on. The third row was never fetched, so it is untouched.

Why the others are wrong:
- *the third replaces the failed one*: the list is fetched once, before the loop.
- *the loop stops*: the catch handles the error and continues.
- *one throw rolls back the batch*: there is no surrounding transaction; each mark is its own write.

excerpts.quote: export async function deliverPendingWebhooks(limit: number) { const deliveries = await listPendingWebhookDeliveries(limit);

readMore.why: The PENDING filter, order and limit.

notes.title: ADMIN and OPS are the same role in practice
notes.body:
`rolePermissions` in `src/lib/permissions.ts` is the single source of truth for RBAC. The OPS and ADMIN entries list the same five permissions in the same order: PAYMENT_CREATE, PAYMENT_READ_ANY, PAYMENT_REFUND, WEBHOOK_DELIVER and RECONCILIATION_RUN. Nothing else in the code checks the role name for extra powers, so "admin" grants nothing beyond OPS.

- RECONCILIATION_RUN, PAYMENT_REFUND and WEBHOOK_DELIVER all appear in the OPS list, so none of the distractors names a permission OPS is missing.
- The "view but not start" and "request but not issue" splits do not exist: a permission is either in the list or not.

excerpts.quote: OPS: [ Permission.PAYMENT_CREATE, Permission.PAYMENT_READ_ANY, Permission.PAYMENT_REFUND, Permission.WEBHOOK_DELIVER, Permission.RECONCILIATION_RUN, ],
`ADMIN` has the same operational permissions as `OPS` in this codebase.

notes.title: A replay repeats the stored status
notes.body:
**Key: 202 again, with the stored body and replayed set to true.**

The first run calls `markIdempotencyCompleted` with `responseStatusCode: 202` and the response body. A later identical request finds the COMPLETED record, and `buildCompletedReplay` returns `record.responseStatusCode ?? 200` (so 202) and the stored body spread with `replayed: true`. The route sends that status with `jsonOk`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *200*: 200 is only the fallback when no status was stored.
- *201 with a new paymentId*: a replay creates nothing.
- *409*: 409 is for a different fingerprint or an unfinished record.

excerpts.quote: statusCode: record.responseStatusCode ?? 200, body: { ...(record.responseBody as Record<string, unknown>), replayed: true,

readMore.why: Where the 202 and the body are stored.

notes.title: Making the ownership branch live needs a customer read route
notes.body:
This goal comes from Exercise 2 in `auth-and-permissions.md`. The ownership code (`buildPaymentListScope()` returning `{ ownerUserId }`) is correct but unreachable, because every read route requires `PAYMENT_READ_ANY`, which CUSTOMER lacks. The matching check therefore asks you to sketch a `GET /api/payments` route guarded by `PAYMENT_READ_OWN` that calls `listVisiblePayments()`, and to say what the existing test guarantees.

The other choices are the checks of the neighbouring exercises: moving `guards.ts` line 32 into a try/catch is Exercise 1 (finding A1), writing down two colliding requests is Exercise 3 (finding A4), and listing where Session rows are deleted is Exercise 4 (session hygiene).

notes.title: Seeing the pattern means listing the reads before each transaction
notes.body:
This is item 3 of the concept check ladder in `concepts-demonstrated.md`. The transaction-scope pattern is about which reads happen before `$transaction` opens. The section "Transactions as a consistency boundary" names four transactions: payment create, webhook processing, refund and reconciliation. The matching check asks you to list the earlier reads for each and say whether a concurrent writer could invalidate them (for refunds and webhooks it can).

The other two choices belong to ladder items 1 and 2: naming the schema line and catch block behind safe concurrent creates, and pointing at the lines that make deliveries atomic and that stop failed ones from being retried.

Payment create (`paymentService.ts:87`), webhook processing (`webhookService.ts:53`), refund (`refundService.ts:36`)

notes.title: Reasoning about A4 means building the colliding pair
notes.body:
Finding A4 says idempotency keys are global: the record is unique on `(route, key)` and the fingerprint hashes only the body. The way to reason about it is concrete: write down two requests (user, key, body) such that user B receives user A's payment id, then name the one-line change in `paymentService.ts` that stops it, such as putting `session.userId` into the fingerprint, which needs no migration.

The other choices belong to the other exercises in the same file: the try/catch around `guards.ts` line 32 (A1), the customer read route that makes the ownership branch live, and the list of places a Session row is deleted.

excerpts.quote: write down the two requests (user, key, body) that cause user B to receive user A's payment id
Fix: include `session.userId` in the unique key or in the fingerprint.

notes.title: Confirming A1 means moving the auth call inside a try
notes.body:
Finding A1: `withRouteAuth()` calls `requirePermission()` at `guards.ts:32`, before the handler runs, so its `RouteError` never reaches the handler's `jsonError()`. To confirm it, you move line 32 into a `try/catch` that returns `jsonError(error)` and check that the SUPPORT call to reconciliation now gets the JSON 403 body, then explain why the handler's own `try` could never catch it.

The other choices are the checks of Exercises 2-4 in `auth-and-permissions.md`: a customer read route for the ownership branch, the colliding requests for A4, and the list of places Session rows are deleted.

excerpts.quote: move line 32 into a `try/catch` that returns `jsonError(error)`
return handler({ request, params, session });

notes.title: Session hygiene starts with where rows are deleted
notes.body:
Sessions are resolved by `getSessionForRequest()`, which treats an expired row as "no session" but never deletes it, so the Session table grows until logout. The hygiene exercise therefore asks you to list every place a Session row is deleted (only `deleteSessionByToken()` via logout, plus the cascade when a user is deleted) and to propose a cleanup for expired sessions.

The other choices are the checks of the neighbouring exercises in `auth-and-permissions.md`: the colliding requests for A4, the try/catch around `guards.ts` line 32 for A1, and the customer read route that makes the ownership branch live.

excerpts.quote: list every place a `Session` row is deleted
Both treat an expired row as "no session" (lines 32 and 56) but never delete it

notes.title: Safe concurrent creates rest on a schema line and a catch block
notes.body:
Ladder item 1 asks why the create path is safe under concurrency. The answer is two pieces of code plus one database behaviour: `@@unique([route, key])` at `prisma/schema.prisma:135`, the `P2002` catch at `paymentService.ts:168-188` that re-reads and replays, and PostgreSQL making an insert that collides with an uncommitted unique row wait. So the matching check asks you to name the schema line, the catch block and that behaviour.

The other choices are ladder items 2 and 3: the outbox-versus-retry lines, and the reads that happen before each of the four transactions.

excerpts.quote: name the schema line and the catch block that together make it safe
In PostgreSQL an `INSERT` that collides with an *uncommitted* row on a unique index waits for the other transaction to finish.

notes.title: Outbox and retry are different properties
notes.body:
An outbox makes the message commit atomically with the business row; retry is about trying again after failure. This repo has the first and not the second. `WebhookDelivery` rows are written in the same create transaction as the payment, and `listPendingWebhookDeliveries` selects only PENDING rows, so a FAILED delivery is never retried. The matching check asks you to point at those two lines.

The other choices are ladder items 1 and 3: the schema line and catch block behind safe concurrent creates, and the reads before each of the four transactions.

excerpts.quote: point to the line that makes delivery rows atomic with payments, and the line that prevents failed rows from being retried
the same shape as a transactional outbox: the "message" commits atomically with the business row

notes.title: The review layer: schema truths, session details and the test record
notes.body:
The later quizzes and flashcards in this pack go beyond the request traces. They draw on the parts of the docs written during the review, which check the code's claims against the code itself.

1. **`docs/architecture/domain-model.md`, second half.** A table that pairs each correctness guarantee with whatever enforces it, a section on individual fields and enum values, a table of the rows each simulation mode writes, and the status lifecycles as implemented. For each guarantee, find the schema line or the service check yourself before reading the table's answer.
2. **`docs/architecture/auth-and-permissions.md`.** The route and page permission matrix and the line-by-line walk from login to a permission decision. Open the cited file for each step before you read the next one.
3. **`docs/learning/testing-rationale.md`, from the 2026-10 re-run on.** What happened when the suite was run again, the table of scratch checks C1 to C14, and the tests worth adding next, in order.
4. **`docs/learning/load-bearing-files.md`, the extra files section** and the corrections that follow it.

Read each claim next to the cited line before you accept it.

excerpts.quote: because in this repo several guarantees live only in the database.
To verify claims in the docs without installing anything

readMore.why: The models, the constraints table and the simulation-mode table.
Which files carry the weight, with what would break if each were wrong.

notes.title: Why an auth failure never reaches the JSON error contract
notes.body:
**Key: the guard throws before the handler runs, outside its try/catch.** `withRouteAuth()` calls `requirePermission()` at `guards.ts:32` and only then calls `handler(...)` at line 34. Every route's `try/catch`, the place where errors become JSON through `jsonError()`, lives inside `handler`. A SUPPORT user without `RECONCILIATION_RUN` makes line 32 throw a `RouteError` that no `try` surrounds, so the documented 403 body is never built; finding A1 says clients get an unstructured 500 instead.

- *A 403 body that Next.js strips*: no JSON body is built in the first place.
- *requirePermission returns false and the handler runs*: it throws, and the handler never runs.
- *jsonError drops the code field*: the error is never passed to `jsonError()` at all.

excerpts.quote: `src/lib/auth/guards.ts:32` throws before `handler(...)` at line 34 runs
The `RouteError` it throws is never passed to `jsonError()`

notes.title: CONFLICT: a status no request ever produces
notes.body:
**Key: only via `markIdempotencyConflict`, a function that nothing calls.** The schema's `IdempotencyStatus` enum lists `CONFLICT`, and `idempotencyRepository.ts:64-72` has a function that would write it. But no code calls that function, so no record ever reaches that status. The domain-model doc lists it among the fields and enum values that look like features and are not.

- *The mismatch branch*: a retry whose body hash differs gets a 409 without the record being touched.
- *The P2002 catch*: a duplicate insert that fails on the unique constraint is turned into a replay, not a conflict mark.
- *The rollback path*: a throw inside the create transaction rolls the record back with everything else; nothing is marked.

excerpts.quote: which nothing calls. Payload mismatches are reported as `409` without touching the record.

notes.title: One wrong client argument can use up a key forever
notes.body:
**Key: the record commits anyway, and the key stays IN_PROGRESS for good.** Today `paymentService.ts:94` passes `tx`, so the idempotency record is part of the create transaction and disappears with it on a rollback. `createIdempotencyRecord` defaults to the global `prisma` client, though. Passed `prisma`, the insert would commit on its own while the payment rolled back, leaving an `IN_PROGRESS` row that no code ever completes. The key is then used up, which is why the doc's blast-radius list names this one-word change.

- *Rolls back with the payment*: that is what happens with `tx`, the case this question rules out.
- *Marked COMPLETED with the error*: completion happens only at the end of a successful transaction.
- *Completed by the next retry*: no code path ever completes a stranded `IN_PROGRESS` row.

excerpts.quote: the record would commit even when the payment rolled back, permanently "using up" the key with an `IN_PROGRESS` row that no code ever completes.
pass `prisma` instead of `tx` → keys stuck `IN_PROGRESS` after rollbacks.

notes.title: Roles are read live on every request
notes.body:
**Key: on their next request, since each request reads the role live.** `findSessionByToken()` loads the session together with its user, and the permission check reads `session.user.role` every time. The session row stores no copy of the role, so a role changed in the database applies to the very next request, with no re-login. That is worth knowing when you debug "why can this user still do X".

- *At the next login*: the role is not copied into the session, so logging in again changes nothing.
- *When the cookie expires*: expiry is irrelevant, because the role is not cached anywhere.
- *At once, because sessions are deleted*: changing a role deletes nothing; session rows go away only at logout.

excerpts.quote: Changing a user's role in the database therefore takes effect on their next request without re-login

notes.title: A constant called SCRYPT_COST that sets the key length
notes.body:
**Key: the derived key length; the cost parameters stay at Node's defaults.** `scryptSync(password, salt, keylen)` takes the output length as its third argument, and `password.ts` passes `SCRYPT_COST` (64) there, so each hash is 64 bytes long. The CPU and memory cost settings would go in an options object, which the code never passes, so Node's defaults apply. The name suggests a tuning knob that is not there.

- *The CPU and memory cost*: those are Node's defaults; nothing raises them.
- *The salt length*: the salt is a separate 16-byte random value.
- *A round count, like a bcrypt work factor*: scrypt has no such argument here, and the value goes to the key length slot.

excerpts.quote: it is passed as the *key length* argument; the scrypt cost parameters are Node's defaults.
scryptSync(password, salt, SCRYPT_COST)

notes.title: Hidden forms are cosmetic; the API permission is the rule
notes.body:
**Key: the API permissions; SUPPORT lacks PAYMENT_CREATE and PAYMENT_REFUND.** The payment pages hide their forms when the role name is SUPPORT, but that only changes what is drawn. A SUPPORT user who sends the request directly is stopped by `withRouteAuth`, because `permissions.ts:22` gives SUPPORT neither permission.

- *The hidden forms*: the doc calls the UI cosmetic; anyone can call the API without the form.
- *A per-record check*: the refund route has none, and create's per-record step is the owner override.
- *The admin layout guard*: it requires `PAYMENT_READ_ANY`, which SUPPORT holds, so SUPPORT gets into `/admin`.

excerpts.quote: the real protection is that `SUPPORT` lacks `PAYMENT_CREATE`/`PAYMENT_REFUND` in `permissions.ts:22`.
`requireStaffPaymentsPage` | `PAYMENT_READ_ANY` | SUPPORT, OPS, ADMIN

notes.title: What a CUSTOMER can really reach today
notes.body:
**Key: create payments, but read none, since every read route needs READ_ANY.** The policy in `permissions.ts` grants CUSTOMER both `PAYMENT_CREATE` and `PAYMENT_READ_OWN`. The route matrix tells a different story: every payment read route and every admin page requires `PAYMENT_READ_ANY`, so the one route a customer can use is `POST /api/payments`. The ownership code is correct, but only tests exercise it; it goes live the day someone adds a customer read route.

- *Read their own through the ownership branch*: no route that a customer can reach calls it.
- *Read but not create*: CUSTOMER holds `PAYMENT_CREATE`; it is reading that is blocked.
- *Create and refund*: refunds need `PAYMENT_REFUND`, which only OPS and ADMIN hold.

excerpts.quote: in practice a customer can only `POST /api/payments` and cannot read anything, not even their own payments.
**The ownership code is unreachable today.**

notes.title: Why commit the transition matrix as a table
notes.body:
**Key: any edit to allowedTransitions must then update an explicit expectation.** Scratch check C5 pushes all 16 (from, to) status pairs through the real `assertAllowedPaymentTransition()` and finds exactly seven allowed. Committed as a table-driven test, that matrix becomes a contract: whoever changes the allowed-edge table also has to change a visible row of expectations, so an accidental new edge cannot slip in quietly.

- *Catches the refund race*: that needs concurrent calls against a real database (the first test on the list); a pure matrix cannot see it.
- *Replaces a check that could not import the guard*: C5 already imports the real function.
- *Proves the schema enforces the edges*: the domain-model doc says nothing in the schema does; the function is the only guard.

excerpts.quote: so a future edit to `allowedTransitions` must update an explicit expectation.
Only `assertAllowedPaymentTransition()`

notes.title: Why npm test fails before a single test runs
notes.body:
**Key: RouteError's constructor parameter properties break strip-only mode.** The `test` script runs Node with `--experimental-strip-types`, which can only erase type annotations. `export class RouteError` in `src/lib/errors.ts` declares `public readonly status` as a constructor parameter property, which is TypeScript-only syntax that also emits code. Three of the four test files fail on it with `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`; the fourth needs zod. So installing zod alone gives no passing run. The cheapest repair is ordinary field declarations and assignments inside the constructor.

- *The glob matches no files*: four files are loaded and fail with specific errors.
- *The flag does not exist*: it runs, and its strip-only mode is what rejects the syntax.
- *A database is needed*: none of the reported errors is about PostgreSQL.

excerpts.quote: TypeScript parameter property is not supported in strip-only mode
rewrite `RouteError` with ordinary field declarations and assignments in the constructor

notes.title: An explicit undefined is not the same as a missing key
notes.body:
**Key: they hash differently; harmless as zod omits absent optional fields.** `stableStringify()` sorts keys but keeps a key whose value is `undefined`, so `{a:1, o:undefined}` and `{a:1}` produce different fingerprints. In this app the hashed body is zod's parsed output, and zod leaves an absent optional field out entirely, so two honest retries never differ this way. The trap is for a caller that builds the body without zod.

- *Same hash because undefined is dropped*: check C4 shows the hashes differ.
- *Same hash, explaining currency replays*: the hashes differ, so C4 explains nothing about any replay.
- *Every UI retry becomes a 409*: the doc calls it harmless here, because zod already omits absent fields.

excerpts.quote: harmless here because zod omits absent optionals, but a trap if a non-zod caller builds the body

notes.title: Same 401, different timing: login enumeration
notes.body:
**Key: response time, since the unknown-email path skips the scrypt work.** `login()` throws the same `401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS` with the same message in both cases (lines 19 and 25), so the response body is no account-enumeration oracle. But for an unknown email it throws straight after the lookup, while for a real account it first runs `verifyPassword()`, a scrypt hash. Measuring how long the failure takes separates the two.

- *A different error code*: both paths return 401 `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`; there is no 404.
- *The body echoes the email*: the body is identical in both cases.
- *A Set-Cookie header*: a session cookie is set only after a successful login, and neither request succeeds.

excerpts.quote: (Timing still differs: the unknown-email path skips the scrypt work.)
throw new RouteError(401, "INVALID_CREDENTIALS", "Email or password is incorrect.");

notes.title: The first test worth adding: two refunds at once
notes.body:
**Key: two concurrent 60-unit refunds via Promise.all; assert exactly one succeeds.** The test creates a 100-unit SUCCEEDED payment and fires two `createRefundForPayment({ amountMinor: 60 })` calls together with `Promise.all`, and it runs against a real database, as the doc requires. It asserts the outcome you want: exactly one refund succeeds. The doc adds that today it would fail, which is the point: it catches Finding L2.

- *Two sequential refunds*: that case already behaves (scratch check C11); the bug needs concurrency.
- *Two concurrent 50-unit refunds ending REFUNDED*: not the test described, and not the assertion it makes.
- *One 120-unit refund failing with 409*: a single request exercises the guard alone, not the race.

excerpts.quote: fire two `createRefundForPayment({ amountMinor: 60 })` calls with `Promise.all`, assert exactly one succeeds. Today it would fail.
